title: The volatility smile
objectives: Read a smile and say what it implies about the risk-neutral distribution.
Correct a digital's price for the smile's slope

screens.title: Two markets
screens.prose: Interviewer: both puts and calls on the same expiry. Why is the 90 strike quoted at a higher vol than the 110? Compare a flat market, 20% everywhere, with the skew. The skew quotes 26% at 70, 22% at 90, 20% at 100 and 18% at 110.
screens.question: Which market charges more for the 70 put, crash protection?

options.text: The skew market: its 70 put is quoted at 26% against 20%
The flat market, since its vol is lower
options.why: At the 70 strike the flat line sits at 20%, below the skew's 26%. A lower vol makes the put cheaper.

options.text: The same, since the at-the-money vol is 20% in both
options.why: You matched the at-the-money point. Crash protection is struck far below it, where the skew is 26%.

hints.text: Compare the two lines at the 70 strike.
A higher quoted vol means a dearer option.
The skew line reads 26% at 70, the flat line 20%.

feedback.correct: The skew market charges more for the 70 put.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read both lines at a strike of 70.

byKey.flat: You read the flat line as higher. At 70 it is the lower of the two.
byKey.same: At-the-money vols match, but the 70 put is far from the money.

explain.text: The skew prices the 70 put at 26% vol, against 20% flat. The market pays more for protection against a crash. Equity puts are dearer than calls of the same distance.

screens.title: The implied density
screens.prose: Each strike's price gives the market's view of where the share ends ($S = 100$, $T = 1$, $r = 0$). The dashed curve is the flat 20% lognormal. The bold curve is the density implied by the skew. Switch between them.
screens.question: Where does the market put more weight than a flat vol does?

options.text: In the left tail, the crash region
In the right tail, the rally region
options.why: You read the skew's peak, which sits right of the flat peak. The right tail is the thinner one.

options.text: In both tails equally
options.why: You assumed a fatter distribution on both sides. This skew moves weight to the left and thins the right.

feedback.correct: The skew has a fatter left tail and a thinner right tail.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two curves far left and far right.

explain.text: Far left the bold curve lies above the dashed one: more weight on crashes. Far right it lies below. Most paths finish a little up and a few fall a long way, with the mean still pinned at 100.

screens.title: How much more likely?
screens.prose: A tight put spread struck at 70 prices the chance of finishing below 70 at $r = 0$. On the skew it gives 8.13%. A flat 20% gives 4.62%.
screens.question: How many times more likely does the market price a fall below 70?

hints.text: Divide the two chances.

feedback.correct: The market prices a crash 1.76 times as likely as a flat vol does.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the skew's chance by the flat chance.

byKey.same: You treated the two chances as equal. They differ by a factor of nearly two.
byKey.vol-ratio: You divided the vols, 26% over 20%. The chance depends on the whole smile, not the ratio of two vols.

explain.text: The ratio is $8.13 \div 4.62 = 1.76$. A higher vol at low strikes, with a falling slope, moves probability into the left tail.

screens.title: The other tail
screens.prose: Now the right tail. The chance of finishing above 130 is 7.90% under a flat 20% and 4.16% on the skew.
screens.question: What does the skew do to the right tail?

options.text: It thins it: less weight on big rallies
It fattens it, as it fattens the left
options.why: You assumed the skew fattens both tails. The right strikes have lower vols, so rallies are cheaper.

options.text: It leaves it unchanged
options.why: You compared only the left tail. Above 130 the chance falls from 7.90% to 4.16%.

hints.text: Compare 7.90% with 4.16%.
A lower vol at the high strikes means cheaper calls.
The skew's 130 vol is 14%, below 20%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two chances above 130.

explain.text: At 130 the skew's vol is 14%, so calls are cheaper and the right tail loses weight: 4.16% against 7.90%.

screens.title: The strike's own vol
screens.prose: A colleague says: the 70 strike's vol is 26%, so price the fall below 70 with a flat 26%. That gives a chance of 10.72%. The tight put spread on the skew gives something else.
screens.question: What is the honest chance of finishing below 70 on the skew, as a fraction?

widget.label: Fraction
widget.accept: 0.0813, from the put spread on the skew

hints.text: Which price gives the chance: a flat vol, or the put spread on the skew?
Earlier you used the spread on the skew.
It was 8.13%, a fraction of 0.0813.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the chance from the put spread on the skew.

byKey.flat-26: You used the strike's own vol for the whole distribution. The smile also tilts, and its slope takes the chance down.

explain.text: A flat 26% gives 10.72%, but the 26% belongs to the 70 strike only. The skew's slope takes $\text{vega} \times 0.002 = 0.0259$ off the flat-vol chance: $0.1072 - 0.0259 = 0.0813$, so the honest chance is 8.13%.

screens.title: The slope's correction
screens.prose: Pushed one step: the digital call is $\Phi(d_2) - \text{vega}\,\sigma'(K)$ along the smile. At the money $\Phi(d_2) = 0.4602$, vega is 39.695 and the slope $\sigma'$ is −0.002 per strike point.
screens.question: By how much does the skew lift the at-the-money digital?

hints.text: The correction is vega times the slope, with the sign.
A falling smile has a negative slope, so minus a negative adds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply vega by the size of the slope.

byKey.no-vega: You said no lift, because the at-the-money vol is the same. The slope still matters.
byKey.slope-only: You gave the slope alone, 0.002. Multiply by vega, 39.695.

explain.text: The skew lifts the digital by $39.695 \times 0.002 = 0.0794$, from 0.4602 to 0.5396. With the forward fixed, a fatter left tail leaves more paths finishing a little up.

screens.title: Differentiate along the smile
screens.prose: Put the lines in order. $BS(K, \sigma)$ is the Black-Scholes call price, $r = 0$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Along the smile the call price is $C(K) = BS(K, \sigma(K))$: the strike enters twice, directly and through the vol
By the chain rule, $-\dfrac{dC}{dK} = -\dfrac{\partial BS}{\partial K} - \text{vega}\cdot\sigma'(K)$
The first term is the flat-vol digital $\Phi(d_2)$, since $-\partial BS/\partial K = \Phi(d_2)$ at $r = 0$. The second is the skew's correction
A falling smile has $\sigma' < 0$, so the correction is positive and $P(S_T > K)$ exceeds the flat-vol chance

hints.text: Write the call price along the smile first.
The strike appears in two places, so use the chain rule.
Price, derivative, name the terms, read the sign.

feedback.correct: The skew's slope times vega is the correction to the flat digital.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the price, differentiate, name the terms, then read the sign.

byKey.b: The chain rule needs the call price along the smile first.

explain.text: The chance of finishing above $K$ is $-dC/dK$ along the smile. With $\sigma' = -0.002$ the correction is positive at every strike.

screens.title: A smile that is a U
screens.prose: Edge case. Currency options often have a U-shaped smile: vols are higher at both wings, with the same at-the-money vol. The figure compares a fat-tailed $t$ with a normal of the same variance.

state.caption: The shape only; no numbers are read from it.

screens.question: What does a U-shaped smile say about the distribution?

options.text: Both tails are fatter than lognormal, with the same at-the-money vol
Both tails are thinner than lognormal
options.why: You read a high wing vol as cheap. A higher vol means a dearer option, so more weight in the tail.

options.text: Only the left tail is fatter, as in equities
options.why: You carried the equity skew over. A U is high at both wings, so both tails are fat.

hints.text: A high vol at the wings means dear wing options.
Dear wing options mean the market puts more weight there.
A U is high on both sides.

feedback.correct: A U says fat tails on both sides.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Higher wing vols mean dearer wings.

explain.text: Dear options at both wings mean more weight in both tails than a lognormal gives. The fat-tailed $t$ has the same variance as the normal but a taller middle and heavier tails.

screens.title: A risk reversal
screens.prose: Interviewer: a client sells the 80 put and buys the 120 call, one year, $r = 0$, share £100. Remember a skew makes puts dearer than calls. Vols: 24% and 16%. Put £2.0317, call £1.1093. About 90 seconds.
screens.question: What premium does she receive? Give a payment as negative.

widget.label: Premium in pounds
widget.accept: £0.92 received: $2.0317 - 1.1093$. Under a flat 20% she would pay £0.96

hints.text: She receives the put's premium and pays the call's.
Subtract the call from the put.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Premium received minus premium paid.

byKey.flat: You used a flat 20% for both legs, where she would pay £0.96. With the skew the put is dearer than the call.
byKey.sign: You reversed the sign. She sells the dear put, so she receives.

explain.text: The skew flips the sign. Under a flat 20% the put is £1.1859 and the call £2.1473, so she would pay £0.96. Say aloud: puts are dear, so selling the put and buying the call pays you.

screens.title: The smile in code
screens.prose: Interviewer: price the digital on the skew two ways. `digital_call_skew` uses the closed form $e^{-rT}\Phi(d_2) - \text{vega}\,\sigma'$ with the vol at $K$. `digital_by_spread` prices a tight call spread, each leg at its own strike's vol.
screens.question: Complete `skew_vol`, `digital_call_skew` and `digital_by_spread`.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. The closed form matches to 5e-6 and the spread to within 1e-5.

hints.text: `skew_vol` is one line: `atm + slope * (K - 100)`.
In the closed form, take the vol at $K$ for $d_1$, $d_2$ and vega.
In the spread, price each leg at the vol of its own strike.

feedback.correct: The closed form and the spread agree on the skew.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check that the vol at $K$ is used throughout, and the sign of the vega term.

explain.text: With slope −0.002 the closed form gives 0.539563 at 100, and the spread agrees within 1e-5. Setting the slope to 0 gives the flat-vol digital.

ideas: A skew with lower vols at higher strikes means dearer puts. That is a fatter left tail and a thinner right tail, with the mean pinned by the forward.
The chance of finishing above $K$ is $-dC/dK$ along the smile, $\Phi(d_2) - \text{vega}\,\sigma'(K)$: the slope corrects the flat-vol chance.
Never price a distribution with one strike's vol: the smile also tilts. A U-shaped smile means fat tails on both sides.

formula.name: Digital on the smile
formula.note: r = 0; a falling smile has a negative slope, so the correction is positive.

summary.trap: A strike's own vol does not price the whole distribution beyond it: use the slope too.

quiz.prose: Vols are 22% at strike 90, 20% at 100 and 18% at 110, same expiry.
quiz.question: Which tail does the market treat as fatter than a flat vol would?

options.text: The left tail: falls below the money
The right tail: rallies above the money
options.why: You read the high vol on the left as a high price for calls. The high vols are on the low strikes, which are puts.

options.text: Neither: the at-the-money vol is the same
options.why: You compared only the middle strike. The wings differ.

feedback.correct: High vols at low strikes mean dear crash protection.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at which strikes carry the high vol.

explain.text: The vol falls as the strike rises, so low strikes, the puts, are dearer. The market puts more weight on large falls.

quiz.prose: A market quotes every strike at the same vol, 20%.
quiz.question: What does that say about the distribution of the share at expiry?

options.text: It is lognormal, as in the Black-Scholes model
It is normal in the share price
options.why: You mixed up the share price and its log. Flat vol means lognormal prices.

options.text: It has fat tails on both sides
options.why: A fat-tailed distribution gives a smile, not a flat line.

feedback.correct: A flat smile is the Black-Scholes world.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Black-Scholes assumes one vol for every strike.

explain.text: One vol at every strike is the lognormal distribution of the model. Any skew or smile is a departure from it.

quiz.prose: Vols: 22% at strike 90 and 18% at strike 110.
quiz.question: In vol terms, what is the 90 put less the 110 call?

options.text: Plus 4 points: the put is quoted at the higher vol
Minus 4 points: the call carries the higher vol
options.why: You reversed the strikes. The lower strike has the higher vol.

options.text: Zero, since both are 10% out of the money
options.why: You matched the distances. The quotes differ by 4 vol points.

feedback.correct: The 90 put is 4 points above the 110 call.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the 110 vol from the 90 vol.

explain.text: 22% less 18% is plus 4 points. That gap is what equity skew means.

quiz.prose: Equity options usually show a skew: low strikes carry higher vols.
quiz.question: Which is a fair reason, with no claim about the future?

options.text: Buyers pay up for crash protection, and a falling share raises a firm's leverage and so its risk
The market expects the share to fall
options.why: You turned a price into a forecast. A skew shows what protection costs, not where the share goes.

options.text: Puts are mispriced and should always be sold
options.why: You assumed the skew is an error. It persists because protection has steady demand.

feedback.correct: Demand for protection and leverage push low strikes up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Name a reason that is about demand or structure, not a forecast.

explain.text: Investors buy puts to hedge, which lifts their price. A fall in the share also raises leverage, so the firm's risk rises when the price falls.
